title: Vichyssoise
subtitle: Cold leek and potato soup with cream
excerpt: A smooth, cold soup of leeks and potato puréed with cream and served chilled. Despite its French name and character, vichyssoise was created in New York in 1917, though it draws directly on the French tradition of potage Parmentier.
sourceNotes: Vichyssoise was created by Louis Diat, a French chef from near Vichy, at the Ritz-Carlton New York in 1917. He based it on a hot leek and potato soup his mother and grandmother made in the Bourbonnais style, which he served cold with additional cream. The hot version, potage Parmentier, is documented in Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903). The dish is now fully absorbed into the French culinary repertoire despite its American origin.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 4 hours ahead; it needs to chill completely. Keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Do not add the cream until just before serving.

content.text: Vichyssoise is the French cold soup. The recipe is a short one, leeks and potato sweated in butter, simmered in stock, blended until smooth, and finished with cream, but the result depends on doing each stage correctly. The leeks must sweat slowly without any colour; the soup must be completely smooth, passed through a sieve after blending; and it must be fully chilled before serving. Serve in chilled bowls with a few fine slices of leek green scattered on top.

items.prepNote: white and pale green parts only, cleaned and sliced
plus a little more to finish

content.text: Melt the butter in the stockpot over low-medium heat. Add the leeks and onion and cook, stirring occasionally, for 15 minutes until completely soft but not coloured at all. If the leeks begin to take any colour, add a splash of water and reduce the heat.
Add the potatoes and stock. Season. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender.
Blend the soup until very smooth.
Pass through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing firmly to extract all liquid.

Chill for at least 4 hours or overnight. The soup will thicken slightly as it cools; thin with a little extra cold stock or water if needed. Taste again for seasoning, chilled food often needs more salt. Serve in cold bowls scattered with chives and a swirl of cream.

items.symptom: The soup has a green or grey tinge
items.cause: The dark green leek tops were included, or the leeks were slightly coloured during sweating.
items.fix: Use only the white and very pale green parts of the leek. The dark green tops give a bitter flavour and a grey colour to the soup. Sweating the leeks should be done very gently, no colour whatsoever.

items.cause: The blended soup was not passed through a sieve.
items.fix: Always pass the blended soup through a fine sieve. Even a powerful blender leaves small fibres from the leeks; the sieve removes them and gives the soup its characteristic silk-smooth texture.

items.symptom: The soup tastes flat when cold
items.cause: Cold dulls flavours; the soup was seasoned at serving temperature rather than for cold.
items.fix: Season the soup after it has chilled. It will need more salt and possibly a small squeeze of lemon juice to brighten the flavour. Always taste the final dish cold before adjusting.

content.text: Louis Diat grew up near Vichy in the Bourbonnais and remembered his grandmother adding cold milk or cream to the leftover leek and potato soup of the day before. As head chef of the Ritz-Carlton New York, he formalized this into the cold, cream-enriched version that appeared on the summer menu in 1917. He named it vichyssoise in reference to the Vichy region of his childhood. It became one of the most copied dishes in American restaurant history. Despite its New York birth, it sits entirely within the French tradition of potage Parmentier, the classic leek-potato soup named for the French agronomist who popularised the potato in France.
